title: The article stuck on the end
goal: Use the Danish definite article — which doesn't stand in front of the noun but sticks to its end — and form plurals.
bekal: turn *en bil* into *bilen* and *et hus* into *huset*
form plurals with three endings: **-er**, **-e**, or no ending
use *den*, *det*, *de*, *her* and *der* to point at things
wave: Go back over **Unit 2** first: cover the Danish, look at the English translation, and rebuild the dialogue. Notice how many verbs simply end in **-r**.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hvor er nøglerne?
dialogs.intro: Morning. Budi is in a rush to get to class. Ahmad stayed the night on the sofa.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Ahmad, have you seen the keys?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Nøglerne? Nej. Er de ikke på bordet?
lines.id: The keys? No. Aren't they on the table?
lines.literal: keys-the? no. are they not on table-the?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bordet er tomt. Og stolen også.
lines.id: The table is empty. And so is the chair.
lines.literal: table-the is empty. and chair-the also.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Kig i tasken. Eller i jakken.
lines.id: Look in the bag. Or in the jacket.
lines.literal: look in bag-the. or in jacket-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jakken hænger ved døren… Nej, den er tom.
lines.id: The jacket's hanging by the door… No, it's empty.
lines.literal: jacket-the hangs by door-the… no, it is empty.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Hvad med vinduet? Du åbnede det i går.
lines.id: What about the window? You opened it yesterday.
lines.literal: what with window-the? you opened it in yesterday.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vent… Her er de! Under avisen.
lines.id: Wait… Here they are! Under the newspaper.
lines.literal: wait… here are they! under newspaper-the.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Selvfølgelig. Det er altid det sidste sted.
lines.id: Of course. It's always the last place you look.
lines.literal: of-course. it is always the last place.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tak! Kan du lukke vinduet, når du går?
lines.id: Thanks! Can you close the window when you leave?
lines.literal: thanks! can you close window-the, when you go?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Ja ja. Og lyset og døren. Jeg kender rutinen.
lines.id: Yes, yes. And the light and the door. I know the routine.
lines.literal: yes yes. and light-the and door-the. I know routine-the.

notes: **This is the unit that matters most.** Danish has no separate word for "the" in front of a noun. The article **sticks to the end**: *en bil* (a car) → *bilen* (the car). No other major language does this apart from its Scandinavian neighbors — English "the" always comes first.
**-en for en-words, -et for et-words.** The article is exactly the same as the indefinite one, just moved: *en* → *-en*, *et* → *-et*. If you know a word's group, you know its ending.

**Spelled -et, said -uhdh.** *Huset* is pronounced **HOO-suhdh**, *bordet* **BOR-uhdh**, *vinduet* **VIN-doo-uhdh**. The *t* in this ending softens into a soft *d*. One of the biggest sound traps for beginners.

**Kig i tasken.** *Kig* is a command — and Danish commands are always **the base form without -r and without at**: *at kigge* → *kig!*, *at komme* → *kom!*, *at lukke* → *luk!* The full rule comes in Unit 11.

**Den er tom** — note *den*, not *det*. *Jakken* is an en-word, so the pronoun replacing it is *den*. If the thing is an et-word, it's *det*: *vinduet… det er lukket*. English has just one "it" for everything.
**Selvfølgelig** is pronounced **sel-FÖL-ee** — the last three letters practically vanish. Long Danish words are almost always shorter in the mouth than on paper.
**Det sidste sted** — notice there's *det* in front **and** the adjective ends in *-e*, but *sted* itself is bare, without an ending. This is called double definiteness; the rule waits in Unit 15.

grammars.title: The definite article: stuck on the back
body: These four rows are the heart of the whole unit. Copy them into your notes and put them somewhere you'll see often.
after: Read the columns left to right: a car → the car → cars → the cars.

Words already ending in *-e* don't add another *e*: *en pige* → *pigen*, not *pigeen*. And words ending in *-el*, *-en*, *-er* drop the middle *e* when an ending is added: *en cykel* → *cyklen* → *cykler*; *et vindue* stays *vinduet*; *en søster* → *søsteren* → *søstre*.
A single final consonant after a short vowel doubles: *et rum* → *rummet*; *en ven* → *vennen* → *venner*.

grammars.title: Forming plurals: three options
body: Danish has three plural endings, and unfortunately there's no reliable rule for choosing one. By far the most common is **-er** — if you have to guess, guess that.

head: Group
Ending
Example
How common
rows: en bil → bil**er**; et æble → æbl**er**
en stol → stol**e**; et hus → hus**e**
et år → to **år**; en ting → to **ting**

after: Group 3 words are almost all very frequent, so they're worth learning in one go: *et år*, *en ting*, *en sko*, *en mus*, *et fjernsyn*, *en fisk*, *et menneske* (→ *mennesker*, which is actually group 1).

Some words change their vowel, like English *man → men*: *en mand → **mænd***, *en bog → **bøger***, *en hånd → **hænder***, *et barn → **børn***, *en nat → **nætter***, *en bonde → **bønder***, *en ko → **køer***.
The definite plural always adds **-ne** to the plural form: *biler* → *bilerne*, *huse* → *husene*, *år* → *årene*, *børn* → *børnene*. This part has no surprises.

grammars.title: Den, det, de — pointing
body: Once nouns have their endings, you still need a way to point at "this one" and "that one".
after: The last two rows are heard far more often in conversation than *denne/dette/disse*, which feel a bit written. If you want to sound natural, use *den her* and *den der*.
⚠️ Once *den/det/de* is used for pointing, the noun **loses its ending**: *den bil*, not *den bilen*. This is the opposite of Norwegian and Swedish, which use both.

sections.title: Eye training: one word, four forms

blocks.text: Read this table out loud, a whole row at a time, from left to right. It's the exercise that looks most boring and works best.

sections.title: Why this feels strange to English speakers

blocks.text: English marks "the" with a separate word in front of the noun, so your instinct is to look for one. That instinct leads to three typical mistakes in class:

items: **Putting a word in front instead of the ending.** *Den bil* looks like "the car", but it means "**that** car". Plain "the car" is *bilen* — no word in front at all.
**Using both at once.** *Den bilen* is wrong. If *den* is already in front, the ending comes off.

The exception that keeps things interesting: jobs (*jeg er lærer*), languages (*jeg taler dansk*) and a number of fixed phrases (*på arbejde*, *i skole*, *til fods*) really do stand bare, sometimes where English would use an article. Learn those phrases whole.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Point at five things around you right now. Say each one in all four forms: *en stol — stolen — stole — stolene*.
If you get stuck, it's not because you don't know the rule yet, but because you don't know the word's group. Go back to the Unit 3 vocabulary list.
